newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong people fear more corruption - survey.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong people fear more corruption - survey.

text.p: Most Hong Kong people believe corruption will increase when the British colony reverts to China, according to a survey conducted by the local anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).

Revealing the results of the ICAC's annual survey to a news conference on Monday, Commissioner Michael Leung said an increased number of people believed graft was common in Hong Kong, where the number of reports of corruption had also grown.
About 69.7 percent of all respondents to the 1996 ICAC survey believed believed the handover on July 1 would cause an increase in corruption,
"This is an issue we are concerned about. To a certain extent, people think that the '97 issue will increase corruption," Leung said.
But he noted that the figure represented a slight drop from 71.7 percent in the 1995 survey.
The survey showed 54.2 percent of respondents considered corruption very common or quite common in Hong Kong. This compares with 50.6 percent in 1995 polls.
About 74.1 percent of the respondents believed that the ICAC should play an increasingly important role in the transition period, compared with 68.4 percent in 1995.
Reports of corruption involving both Hong Kong and Chinese parties increased by three percent year-on-year to 114 cases in the first nine months.
Although this was still low, Leung warned that there could be bigger problems ahead.

"There could be collusion between the various more important agencies on either side which involves a number of activities including smuggling, vice establishments, prostitution and drugs. All this is interrelated with corruption and bribery on both sides of the border," he said.
Overall, reports of corruption, excluding those involving elections, were up three percent year-on-year to 2,297 cases from January to September, 1996.
About 60.4 percent of the respondents to the survey considered corruption very common or quite common in the business sector. This compares with 59.1 percent in 1995.
